title: Kare-Kare
subtitle: filipino peanut stew
excerpt: Kare-kare is a Filipino stew of slow-cooked beef in a rich, thick peanut sauce with aubergine, cabbage, and carrots. It is traditionally served with fermented shrimp paste on the side. Serves 4.
sourceNotes: Kare-kare is a festive Filipino dish with origins thought to trace back to the Pampanga region of Luzon. It is traditionally made with oxtail; beef shin gives a similar result and is more widely available.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze the stew without the vegetables for up to 3 months. Add fresh vegetables when reheating.
recipe.batchNotes: Make a large batch of the stew base. The peanut sauce keeps well and the vegetables can be added fresh each time.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The stew base improves overnight. Reheat gently and add the vegetables fresh.

glossaryTerms.definition: A Filipino stew with a thick peanut sauce, traditionally made with oxtail and served with bagoong, a fermented shrimp paste.
Filipino fermented shrimp paste. Served as a condiment alongside kare-kare; its saltiness and pungency cuts through the richness of the peanut sauce.

content.text: is a rich, slow-cooked stew that takes patience. The beef needs at least 2 hours to become properly tender in the peanut broth. Traditional versions are served with
on the side; a small spoonful stirred into the stew adds a hit of salt and umami. Serves 4.
The peanut sauce is blended smooth. It thickens as it cooks, so add stock to loosen if it becomes too thick before the meat is tender.
Heat the oil in a stockpot over medium-high heat. Brown the beef in batches until seared on all sides. Remove and set aside.
Reduce heat to medium. Add the onion and garlic. Cook for 3 minutes until softened. Add the turmeric and stir for 1 minute.
Blend the peanuts with 200ml of the water until smooth. Add to the pot along with the remaining water and the beef. Bring to a simmer.
Cover and simmer over low heat for 90 minutes, stirring occasionally. Add more water if the sauce becomes too thick.
Add the carrot and aubergine. Cook uncovered for 15 minutes. Add the cabbage and cook for a further 5 minutes.
Stir in the fish sauce. Taste and adjust. Serve over rice topped with spring onion.

attrs.problem: The peanut sauce is too thick and catching on the bottom.
attrs.solution: Add hot water 100ml at a time and stir well. Keep the heat low and the lid on during the long simmer stage.

attrs.problem: The beef is still chewy at 90 minutes.
attrs.solution: Continue cooking. Shin is a tough cut and some pieces take up to 2.5 hours. The sauce gets better the longer it goes.
Add more fish sauce. The peanut base needs enough salt to bring it to life. Stir in a teaspoon of fish sauce at a time until the flavour opens up.

content.text: Kare-kare is a Filipino celebration dish associated with special occasions and family gatherings. It is thought to have originated in Pampanga, known as the culinary capital of the Philippines. The dish is always served with steamed rice and a small bowl of bagoong. Fermented shrimp paste can be found in Filipino and Southeast Asian grocery stores.
